screens.title: Project 7: The Complete VM Translator
screens.narratorSegment: This final project completes the VM translator that sits between the Jack compiler and your assembler. You already created pieces of this pipeline: the Jack compiler produces VM code, and the assembler converts assembly to machine code. Project 7 ties those pieces together by requiring a translator that implements every VM command, includes bootstrap initialization, and supports multiple VM files in one directory. Successfully translating Pong or Tetris and running them in the Computer Simulator is a milestone: you will see an interactive program run on hardware you designed from simple logic gates. In practical terms, the translator expands each compact VM command into a sequence of Hack assembly instructions that the C P U understands. That expansion makes the generated assembly verbose, but it also preserves portability and separates concerns. As you complete this project you'll test correctness with a suite of programs, inspect the call stack and memory map while games run, and reflect on how abstraction layers let us build complex systems from simple parts. Think about what changed for you when you first saw a moving ball or a falling Tetris piece — that experience ties together every step you've taken so far.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this project you will have a functioning VM translator that implements the full VM instruction set, including arithmetic, memory access, program flow, function call semantics, bootstrap initialization, and handling multiple VM files in one directory. You will test your translator using a standardized suite: SimpleFunction, NestedCall, FibonacciElement, StaticsTest, Pong, and Tetris. Each test verifies different behaviors — from basic calls to large interactive games — so you gain confidence the translator works across simple to complex programs. You will also learn how to run the translator, assemble the generated assembly, and run the resulting machine code in the Computer Simulator to observe runtime state such as the call stack and memory segments. Finally, you will reflect on the full toolchain and write a short report describing translation time, generated assembly size, and what surprised you. These skills matter because they turn small components into a working system and teach the practice of testing at increasing scales. A verified milestone demonstrates both correctness and an understanding of abstraction layers.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Testing & Reflection
Testing workflow
Follow this sequence for each test directory:
  1. Run the VM translator on the directory to produce a single .asm file.
  2. Assemble the .asm file into a .hack binary.
  3. Load the .hack file into the Computer Simulator and execute the program.
  4. Observe the call stack, stack pointer, and memory segments during execution.
Measurement checklist
  • Record translation time for Pong and Tetris.
  • Count lines of generated assembly.
  • Measure run time steps or frames in the simulator.
Key Takeaway

Concrete measurements help you reason about abstraction cost and identify hotspots for optimization or debugging.

screens.title: What the VM Translator Must Implement
screens.narratorSegment: Project 7 defines a precise contract. The translator must implement all arithmetic commands, memory access commands for every segment, program flow commands, function-call commands, bootstrap initialization, and directory-level handling of multiple VM files. Each item maps to a testing target. Arithmetic commands translate stack operations such as addition, subtraction, negation, logical operations, and comparisons into sequences of assembly instructions that manipulate the Hack stack pointer and memory. Memory access commands — push and pop — require careful handling of segments like local, argument, this, that, constant, static, pointer, and temp; each segment has distinct addressing rules that your translator must encode. Program flow commands label, goto, and if-goto map to symbolic labels in assembly with unique names to avoid collisions across functions and files. Function commands — function, call, and return — implement call frame setup and teardown, preserving return addresses, arguments, and local variables. Bootstrap code initializes the stack pointer and optionally calls the system's entry point so programs with functions start correctly. Finally, handling multiple VM files means the translator must merge translated code into one assembly file and manage static variable names so they remain file-scoped. A single missing piece can break a complex test like Pong or Tetris, so implement carefully and test each component in isolation before running the full games.

content.html:
Core Concept › VM Translator Requirements

Definition & checklist

  • Arithmetic commands: add, sub, neg, eq, gt, lt, and, or, not.
  • Memory access: push/pop across local, argument, this, that, constant, static, pointer, temp.
  • Program flow: label, goto, if-goto with function-scoped labels.
  • Function commands: function, call, return—correct call-frame handling.
  • Bootstrap code: initialize SP and call Sys.init when required.
  • Multi-file: translate multiple .vm files into a single .asm output with proper scoping.
Common misconception

The VM is not a one-to-one mapping to assembly. Expect each VM command to expand into several assembly instructions; the translator's job is to produce correct sequences, not minimal ones.

Key Takeaway

Treat Project 7 as a checklist of behaviors to implement and verify. Each feature maps to observable runtime behavior in tests.

Annotated examples

VM snippet
push constant 5
push constant 3
add
Generated assembly (conceptual)
// push constant 5
@5
D=A
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
// push constant 3
@3
D=A
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
// add
@SP
AM=M-1
D=M
A=A-1
M=M+D
Example scenario
Constant arithmetic maps to stack ops

A single add requires popping two values, adding, and pushing the result. Mistakenly leaving SP incorrect breaks later code.

Check your understanding

Why must labels be unique per function? What happens to return addresses when call frames are nested?

screens.title: Bootstrap and Multi-file Translation
screens.narratorSegment: Bootstrap and multi-file handling are small but essential pieces. Bootstrap code initializes the stack pointer to the standard address and typically calls the system's entry routine — often Sys. init — to set the program in motion. Without bootstrap the stack pointer may point to an undefined location and function calls will fail. When translating multiple VM files in a directory, the translator must concatenate translated code into a single assembly file. Static variables require file-scoped names so that two files with a static variable named the same do not collide; a common approach is to prefix the static symbol with the originating file's base name. Also ensure label generation avoids collisions across files and functions by namespacing labels with function names and unique counters. A robust process: 1) write bootstrap code at the top of the output; 2) for each VM file, translate commands and append to the single output; 3) ensure every generated label/symbol is uniquely namespaced. Test this workflow with StaticsTest and multi-file projects. A key misconception is thinking bootstrap is optional: it is required when translated programs rely on an initialized stack or when calling conventions expect a starting frame. Confirm bootstrap behavior by running small programs that use function calls immediately after start.

keyIdea.text: Bootstrap initializes runtime state; multi-file translation must preserve file-scoped statics and produce unique labels so combined output runs correctly.

content.html:
Process Flow › Bootstrap & Files
Process steps
  1. Emit bootstrap: set SP and call Sys.init if required.
  2. Iterate VM files: translate and append to a single .asm output.
  3. Namespace statics: prefix static symbols with file name.
  4. Generate unique labels using function names and counters.
  5. Assemble and run the resulting .asm in the simulator.
Example naming

File A's static variable number 3 → A.static.3. File B's static 3 → B.static.3. This prevents cross-file collisions when both are linked into one assembly file.

Pitfall

Appending files without namespacing statics or labels causes subtle runtime errors when games depend on isolated static storage.

Top/bottom example
A minimal bootstrap sequence in conceptual assembly form:
// bootstrap
@256
D=A
@SP
M=D
// call Sys.init
@Sys.init.return.0
D=A
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
@Sys.init
0;JMP
(Sys.init.return.0)
Check your understanding

If you omit bootstrap and a program immediately calls a function, what observable simulator errors might you see? How would you detect an SP problem?

screens.title: Function Call and Return Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: Function calls are the most intricate translator target because they manipulate the stack and several pointers to create a call frame. The translator must implement the call sequence: push the return address, push LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT, reposition ARG for the callee, set LCL to SP, and jump to the called function. On return, it must restore the caller's frame: set a frame pointer, retrieve the return address from the saved frame, reposition the return value, restore THAT, THIS, ARG, LCL, and jump to the saved return address. This sequence preserves local variables and arguments across nested calls. A concrete example: calling a function that takes two arguments will push the return address and saved pointers, then place the arguments so the callee finds them at ARG. A common bug is miscalculating ARG or forgetting to update LCL; either mistake corrupts local variables and causes incorrect behavior in nested calls. Another misconception is thinking return is symmetrical to call; in practice return does more work because it must recover the caller’s environment precisely. When you run NestedCall and FibonacciElement, inspect the call stack in the simulator: you should see frames push and pop in the expected order and return values move to the caller's stack frame. If a test fails, step through the assembly around call and return sequences to verify each saved pointer and the return address handling.

keyIdea.text: Correct call and return sequences preserve caller state and place arguments and return values at the correct addresses; errors here break nested and recursive calls.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Function Calls
Call sequence (conceptual VM → assembly mapping)
// VM: call MyFunc 2
// assembly outline (conceptual)
@return-address
D=A
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
@LCL
D=M
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
// push ARG, THIS, THAT similarly
// ARG = SP - 5 - nArgs
// LCL = SP
@MyFunc
0;JMP
(return-address)
Concrete check

When a callee returns, the translator must move the return value to the caller's stack location and restore saved pointers in the right order to recover the caller environment.

Debugging tips
  • Inspect SP and LCL values before and after calls to ensure correct updates.
  • Set temporary labels for return addresses with unique counters to avoid collisions.
  • Use small test programs with known return values to validate behavior before running large games.
Pitfall

Miscalculating ARG (for example off by one) is the most common mistake in call/return implementation.

screens.title: Memory Segments and Static Variables
screens.narratorSegment: The VM exposes several memory segments each with distinct addressing behavior. Local and argument are based on LCL and ARG pointers and refer to per-function storage. This and that point to areas used by objects and OS abstractions. Temp maps to fixed registers and has limited size. Pointer is a small segment used to set THIS and THAT. Constant is a virtual segment that does not access memory — push constant just loads an immediate value onto the stack. Static variables are the most delicate: each static variable in a. vm file should map to a unique assembly symbol scoped to that file. If two files both declare static 5, the translator must produce distinct symbols (e. g., FileA. static.5 and FileB. static.5) so they do not clash when combined into one. asm. A practical example: implementing push static 3 should generate an assembly symbol that reads and writes a file-scoped R A M location. A common misconception is treating static as global without file context; that will cause cross-file interference in larger projects. When testing StaticsTest, verify that updating static variables in one module does not affect another — the simulator memory map will show separate storage if namespacing is correct. Correct segment handling ensures that the runtime invariants required by higher-level code hold true during complex executions like Pong or Tetris.

keyIdea.text: Each VM segment has unique addressing rules; static variables must be file-scoped symbols to prevent cross-file collisions.

content.html:
Definition › Memory Segments
Segment reference
  • local — relative to LCL, per-function locals.
  • argument — relative to ARG, where parameters live.
  • this / that — object or OS memory regions.
  • temp — fixed small area in RAM, limited indexes.
  • pointer — directly sets THIS or THAT.
  • constant — immediate values; no memory access.
  • static — file-scoped variables mapped to named symbols.
Example

push static 3 in file Foo.vm → access Foo.static.3. This preserves independence between Foo and other files.

Concrete code example
// VM: push static 3 (in Foo.vm)
@Foo.static.3
D=M
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
Check StaticsTest: write into Foo.static.3 and read it back after calling functions from another file. If values clash, static naming is incorrect.

screens.title: VM Abstraction vs Generated Assembly
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing VM code to generated assembly clarifies a common question: why is the assembly so much longer? VM commands are compact, high-level stack operations that the translator implements with multiple low-level instructions because the Hack hardware lacks native VM primitives. For example, a single VM add turns into several assembly lines that decrement SP, fetch operands, compute, and store results. The expansion is intentional: VM code is compact and easy for compilers to emit, while the translator maps those semantics to machine-level operations. Does verbose generated assembly mean inefficiency? Not necessarily. The translator's static expansion is simple and correct; optimizations could reduce instruction counts, but the translator prioritizes clarity and portability for this course. Real systems apply just-in-time compilation or backend optimization to produce faster code, but those techniques are beyond this project. A misconception to avoid is equating expansion with poor design — instead, see it as a layered approach that trades manual assembly authoring for automated, repeatable translation. For large programs like Tetris, the translator may produce tens of thousands of assembly lines, which is normal for a straightforward static translator. The important measure is correctness: if Pong or Tetris runs correctly, the translator fulfills its educational purpose.

screens.title: Testing Workflow and Debugging Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Testing the complete translator is a disciplined workflow: translate, assemble, run, observe, and iterate. Start by running the translator on small test directories like SimpleFunction and NestedCall. Assemble the generated. asm into a. hack file and load it in the Computer Simulator. Use the simulator's step and run controls to watch the stack pointer, memory segments, and call stack evolve. For debugging, isolate failing behavior: create a minimal VM program that reproduces the issue and translate just that file. Compare the translator's assembly to a known-correct reference to find mismatches. Logging intermediate translator steps — for example, printing generated labels or instruction counts — helps localize mistakes. For performance issues such as very long translation times on large programs, measure stages: parsing, code generation, and file input and output. A practical tip: run StaticsTest before Pong or Tetris to ensure your static-naming scheme works. When testing Pong or Tetris, pay attention to input handling, graphics routines, and animation loops; a single miscompiled memory access can break user input or rendering logic. Always include a hypothesis about the bug and a small experiment to confirm or refute it. This scientific approach shortens debugging cycles and increases confidence in the final translator.

Architecture › Testing Workflow
Repeatable process
1. Translate
2. Assemble
3. Run & observe
For debugging: reproduce the error with a minimal VM example, compare your assembly to a reference, and iterate on fixes. Log unique label generation and static naming to confirm scoping rules.

Measurement cards
Translation time

screens.title: Pong: Why It Proves the Translator
screens.narratorSegment: Pong is the first large program you'll run to validate the translator. It combines object-oriented code, graphics, keyboard input, and a real-time game loop. Running Pong verifies many translator features at once: object memory access, correct static handling, program flow for animation loops, and function call discipline for game logic. When Pong runs correctly, you will see moving objects, respond to keyboard input, and observe the call stack changing as the game updates. To inspect correctness, focus on rendering and input code paths: a single incorrect memory access can make the ball not draw or ignore keyboard events. Use the simulator to watch memory addresses used by the screen buffer and verify they receive expected writes during draw calls. If Pong crashes or hangs, reproduce the failure with a smaller VM program that touches the same segments or call pattern, then step through the generated assembly. Pong is also a morale moment: seeing animation on your self-built computer confirms end-to-end correctness, but remember it depends on many small pieces working together — miscompiling a single VM command is often the root cause of a failure.

screens.title: Tetris: The Ultimate Integration Test
screens.narratorSegment: Tetris is the most challenging test in the suite because it combines multiple game states, complex graphics, rotation logic, line clearing, and persistent score/level tracking. It stresses nearly every translator feature and the runtime's correctness. Because Tetris contains menus, game state transitions, and continuous input processing, small mistakes in memory addressing or call-frame handling often manifest as crashes, stuck pieces, or incorrect rendering. Approach validation incrementally: first confirm static naming and simple graphics routines, then test piece rotation and line clearing with isolated VM snippets. Measure the generated assembly size and translation time to ensure the translator completes on reasonable inputs. When Tetris runs correctly, you will see state machines for menus and gameplay and watch the call stack evolve as functions handle input and update the board. A common misconception is that Tetris errors are necessarily algorithmic; many are translation bugs. Debug systematically: isolate failing behavior, reproduce with a minimal VM example, and step through the corresponding assembly. If Tetris runs, you have strong evidence the toolchain handles real-world program complexity and that abstraction layers from Jack through VM to hardware are functioning together.

screens.title: The Software Stack — Six Layers of Abstraction
screens.narratorSegment: A clear assessment checks whether you can identify and explain the six abstraction layers in this toolchain. From top to bottom they are: Jack, the high-level language providing objects, methods, and control structures; VM code, a stack-based intermediate representation that abstracts registers and memory; Assembly, the symbolic low-level code with labels and mnemonics; Machine code, the binary instructions executed by the C P U; C P U microarchitecture, the ALU, registers, and control logic that implement instructions; and logic gates, the physical Nand-based building blocks. Each layer hides complexity and offers services to the layer above: Jack programmers do not manage call frames manually because the compiler and VM handle it; the VM translator emits assembly so the assembler does not need to parse high-level constructs; the C P U executes machine code without knowledge of source-level abstractions. For assessment, explain the purpose of each layer and give a short example of what it shields the layer above from. A common misconception is that more layers always slow down programs; while additional layers may add overhead, they also enable portability, modularity, and productivity. In practice, optimization at different layers mitigates performance costs while preserving these benefits.

Assessment › Abstraction Layers
Layer hierarchy
Jack
High-level language with classes and methods. Shields programmers from manual stack management.
VM
Stack-based intermediate code that abstracts hardware details and enables portability.
Assembly
Symbolic instructions and labels, one step away from machine code.
Machine code
Binary instructions executed by the CPU.

ALU, registers, and control logic that implement machine instructions.

Nand-based circuits that implement the CPU primitives.

Describe each layer's purpose and give one concrete example of what it hides from the layer above. Explain why these abstractions are essential for building complex systems.

fullNarratorScript:
This final project completes the VM translator that sits between the Jack compiler and your assembler. You already created pieces of this pipeline: the Jack compiler produces VM code, and the assembler converts assembly to machine code. Project 7 ties those pieces together by requiring a translator that implements every VM command, includes bootstrap initialization, and supports multiple VM files in one directory. Successfully translating Pong or Tetris and running them in the Computer Simulator is a milestone: you will see an interactive program run on hardware you designed from simple logic gates. In practical terms, the translator expands each compact VM command into a sequence of Hack assembly instructions that the C P U understands. That expansion makes the generated assembly verbose, but it also preserves portability and separates concerns. As you complete this project you'll test correctness with a suite of programs, inspect the call stack and memory map while games run, and reflect on how abstraction layers let us build complex systems from simple parts. Think about what changed for you when you first saw a moving ball or a falling Tetris piece — that experience ties together every step you've taken so far.

By the end of this project you will have a functioning VM translator that implements the full VM instruction set, including arithmetic, memory access, program flow, function call semantics, bootstrap initialization, and handling multiple VM files in one directory. You will test your translator using a standardized suite: SimpleFunction, NestedCall, FibonacciElement, StaticsTest, Pong, and Tetris. Each test verifies different behaviors — from basic calls to large interactive games — so you gain confidence the translator works across simple to complex programs. You will also learn how to run the translator, assemble the generated assembly, and run the resulting machine code in the Computer Simulator to observe runtime state such as the call stack and memory segments. Finally, you will reflect on the full toolchain and write a short report describing translation time, generated assembly size, and what surprised you. These skills matter because they turn small components into a working system and teach the practice of testing at increasing scales. A verified milestone demonstrates both correctness and an understanding of abstraction layers.

This objective page drills into the practical skills you'll use to verify the translator. First, you will run the translator on each test directory and then assemble and execute the produced assembly file in the Computer Simulator. Observe the call stack and memory segments while SimpleFunction and NestedCall exercise function-call mechanics, FibonacciElement exercises recursion, and StaticsTest validates static variables across files. Pong and Tetris stress the full stack: they exercise graphics, input, animation, and complex control flow. Second, you will take measurements: how long translation takes, how many assembly lines are produced, and how long each game runs on the simulator. These numbers help you judge performance and the cost of abstraction. Third, you will write a reflection tying technical observations to conceptual insights about abstraction layers and toolchain design. A good reflection explains what surprised you, what was hard, and what you found most rewarding. That practice is essential — building a system is only complete when you can evaluate and explain it.

Project 7 defines a precise contract. The translator must implement all arithmetic commands, memory access commands for every segment, program flow commands, function-call commands, bootstrap initialization, and directory-level handling of multiple VM files. Each item maps to a testing target. Arithmetic commands translate stack operations such as addition, subtraction, negation, logical operations, and comparisons into sequences of assembly instructions that manipulate the Hack stack pointer and memory. Memory access commands — push and pop — require careful handling of segments like local, argument, this, that, constant, static, pointer, and temp; each segment has distinct addressing rules that your translator must encode. Program flow commands label, goto, and if-goto map to symbolic labels in assembly with unique names to avoid collisions across functions and files. Function commands — function, call, and return — implement call frame setup and teardown, preserving return addresses, arguments, and local variables. Bootstrap code initializes the stack pointer and optionally calls the system's entry point so programs with functions start correctly. Finally, handling multiple VM files means the translator must merge translated code into one assembly file and manage static variable names so they remain file-scoped. A single missing piece can break a complex test like Pong or Tetris, so implement carefully and test each component in isolation before running the full games.

Bootstrap and multi-file handling are small but essential pieces. Bootstrap code initializes the stack pointer to the standard address and typically calls the system's entry routine — often Sys. init — to set the program in motion. Without bootstrap the stack pointer may point to an undefined location and function calls will fail. When translating multiple VM files in a directory, the translator must concatenate translated code into a single assembly file. Static variables require file-scoped names so that two files with a static variable named the same do not collide; a common approach is to prefix the static symbol with the originating file's base name. Also ensure label generation avoids collisions across files and functions by namespacing labels with function names and unique counters. A robust process: 1) write bootstrap code at the top of the output; 2) for each VM file, translate commands and append to the single output; 3) ensure every generated label/symbol is uniquely namespaced. Test this workflow with StaticsTest and multi-file projects. A key misconception is thinking bootstrap is optional: it is required when translated programs rely on an initialized stack or when calling conventions expect a starting frame. Confirm bootstrap behavior by running small programs that use function calls immediately after start.

Function calls are the most intricate translator target because they manipulate the stack and several pointers to create a call frame. The translator must implement the call sequence: push the return address, push LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT, reposition ARG for the callee, set LCL to SP, and jump to the called function. On return, it must restore the caller's frame: set a frame pointer, retrieve the return address from the saved frame, reposition the return value, restore THAT, THIS, ARG, LCL, and jump to the saved return address. This sequence preserves local variables and arguments across nested calls. A concrete example: calling a function that takes two arguments will push the return address and saved pointers, then place the arguments so the callee finds them at ARG. A common bug is miscalculating ARG or forgetting to update LCL; either mistake corrupts local variables and causes incorrect behavior in nested calls. Another misconception is thinking return is symmetrical to call; in practice return does more work because it must recover the caller’s environment precisely. When you run NestedCall and FibonacciElement, inspect the call stack in the simulator: you should see frames push and pop in the expected order and return values move to the caller's stack frame. If a test fails, step through the assembly around call and return sequences to verify each saved pointer and the return address handling.

The VM exposes several memory segments each with distinct addressing behavior. Local and argument are based on LCL and ARG pointers and refer to per-function storage. This and that point to areas used by objects and OS abstractions. Temp maps to fixed registers and has limited size. Pointer is a small segment used to set THIS and THAT. Constant is a virtual segment that does not access memory — push constant just loads an immediate value onto the stack. Static variables are the most delicate: each static variable in a. vm file should map to a unique assembly symbol scoped to that file. If two files both declare static 5, the translator must produce distinct symbols (e. g., FileA. static.5 and FileB. static.5) so they do not clash when combined into one. asm. A practical example: implementing push static 3 should generate an assembly symbol that reads and writes a file-scoped R A M location. A common misconception is treating static as global without file context; that will cause cross-file interference in larger projects. When testing StaticsTest, verify that updating static variables in one module does not affect another — the simulator memory map will show separate storage if namespacing is correct. Correct segment handling ensures that the runtime invariants required by higher-level code hold true during complex executions like Pong or Tetris.

Comparing VM code to generated assembly clarifies a common question: why is the assembly so much longer? VM commands are compact, high-level stack operations that the translator implements with multiple low-level instructions because the Hack hardware lacks native VM primitives. For example, a single VM add turns into several assembly lines that decrement SP, fetch operands, compute, and store results. The expansion is intentional: VM code is compact and easy for compilers to emit, while the translator maps those semantics to machine-level operations. Does verbose generated assembly mean inefficiency? Not necessarily. The translator's static expansion is simple and correct; optimizations could reduce instruction counts, but the translator prioritizes clarity and portability for this course. Real systems apply just-in-time compilation or backend optimization to produce faster code, but those techniques are beyond this project. A misconception to avoid is equating expansion with poor design — instead, see it as a layered approach that trades manual assembly authoring for automated, repeatable translation. For large programs like Tetris, the translator may produce tens of thousands of assembly lines, which is normal for a straightforward static translator. The important measure is correctness: if Pong or Tetris runs correctly, the translator fulfills its educational purpose.
